cls: Urinary alkalinizer / oral alkali (citrate salt of potassium)
quick: Severe hypocitraturia: 60 mEq/day; mild-moderate: 30 mEq/day, in divided doses
Take with meals or within 30 minutes after meals or a bedtime snack
No animal studies; give only if clearly needed
Give to a breastfeeding woman only if clearly needed
Avoid in chronic renal failure/impaired potassium excretion (hyperkalemia)
No specific interaction described in labeling
Serum potassium, urinary citrate and pH, renal function, ECG if at risk
summary: Potassium citrate is an oral alkali (citrate salt of potassium) used to manage renal tubular acidosis with calcium stones, hypocitraturic calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis of any etiology, and uric acid lithiasis (with or without calcium stones). By delivering an absorbable alkali load, it raises urinary citrate and urine pH, reducing the saturation of stone-forming calcium and uric acid salts. The goal is to restore urinary citrate (>320 mg/day, toward ~640 mg/day) and raise urine pH to 6.0-7.0. Dosing depends on severity of hypocitraturia (typically 30-60 mEq/day in divided doses with meals). Because it is a potassium salt, it is CONTRAINDICATED in hyperkalemia or conditions predisposing to it, and potentially fatal hyperkalemia can develop and may be asymptomatic. The wax-matrix extended-release tablets are also contraindicated when GI transit is delayed (risk of GI lesions) and in peptic ulcer disease.
indications: Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) with calcium stones
Hypocitraturic calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis of any etiology
Uric acid lithiasis with or without calcium stones

dosage.d: Initiate at 60 mEq/day - 30 mEq twice daily or 20 mEq three times daily
dosage.n: With meals or within 30 minutes after meals or bedtime snack

dosage.c: Mild to moderate hypocitraturia (urinary citrate >150 mg/day)
dosage.d: Initiate at 30 mEq/day - 15 mEq twice daily or 10 mEq three times daily
dosage.n: Titrate to urinary citrate and pH goals; with food

admin: Swallow the extended-release tablets whole; do not crush or chew the wax-matrix tablets
Take with meals or within 30 minutes after meals or a bedtime snack to limit GI irritation
Combine with a regimen that limits dietary salt and encourages high fluid intake (urine output at least 2 L/day)
Titrate the dose to achieve urinary citrate above 320 mg/day (toward ~640 mg/day) and urine pH 6.0-7.0
Patients may notice intact tablet matrices (ghost tablets) in the stool - this is expected
moa: Potassium citrate provides an absorbable alkali load. When metabolized, citrate consumes hydrogen ion and is converted to bicarbonate, raising the systemic and urinary pH and increasing urinary citrate excretion. Increased urinary citrate complexes calcium (reducing calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate saturation), and the higher urine pH increases the solubility of uric acid - together inhibiting the formation of calcium and uric acid stones.

absolute: Hyperkalemia or conditions predisposing to it (e.g., chronic renal failure, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, acute dehydration, strenuous exercise in unconditioned persons, adrenal insufficiency, extensive tissue breakdown, or use of potassium-sparing agents)
Conditions causing arrest or delay of tablet passage through the GI tract (delayed gastric emptying, esophageal compression, intestinal obstruction or stricture, or anticholinergic use)
Active urinary tract infection (with urea-splitting or other organisms) associated with calcium or struvite stones
relative: Concurrent potassium-sparing diuretics or RAAS inhibitors
Conditions causing volume depletion or acidosis with potassium shifts

preg: Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted. It is not known whether potassium citrate can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. Potassium citrate should be given to a pregnant woman only if clearly needed.
lact: The normal potassium content of human milk is about 13 mEq/L, and it is not known whether potassium citrate alters this. Potassium citrate should be given to a breastfeeding woman only if clearly needed.
renal: Use is contraindicated or hazardous in patients with impaired potassium excretion (e.g., chronic renal failure), where potassium citrate can produce hyperkalemia and cardiac arrest. Avoid in significant renal impairment; if used, monitor serum potassium closely.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is described in the labeling.

major: Potassium-sparing diuretics (triamterene, spironolactone, amiloride) - avoid concomitant use; risk of severe hyperkalemia
moderate: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) - monitor for hyperkalemia
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) - monitor for hyperkalemia
Drugs that slow GI transit, such as anticholinergics - increase GI irritation from potassium salts
minor: Other potassium-containing supplements or salt substitutes (additive potassium load)
interactions.food: Take with meals or shortly after to minimize GI irritation; high dietary salt should be limited.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is described in the labeling.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor serum potassium, renal function, urinary citrate and pH; ECG if hyperkalemia is suspected (peaked T waves, loss of P wave, widened QRS).

common: Intact tablet matrices visible in stool
serious: Gastrointestinal lesions - ulceration, bleeding, perforation, or obstruction (wax-matrix tablets)
emergency: GI bleeding, severe abdominal pain, or signs of bowel perforation/obstruction

monitoring: Serum potassium periodically and when clinically indicated
Renal function (especially in those at risk of impaired potassium excretion)
24-hour urinary citrate and urine pH to guide dosing
GI symptoms; discontinue immediately for severe vomiting, abdominal pain, or GI bleeding and evaluate for perforation/obstruction
ECG in patients at risk for hyperkalemia
counsel: Swallow the tablets whole with a full glass of water; do not crush or chew them
Take with food or just after a meal to reduce stomach upset, and drink plenty of fluids
It is normal to see the empty tablet shell in your stool
Stop and seek care for severe stomach pain, vomiting, black or bloody stools, irregular heartbeat, muscle weakness, or tingling
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless your doctor approves
pk: Urinary citrate and pH rise within hours of dosing; sustained with regular dosing
Extended-release wax matrix releases potassium and citrate gradually over hours
Citrate is rapidly metabolized to bicarbonate; potassium handling depends on renal function
Divided dosing 2-3 times daily maintains urinary alkalinization
Store at controlled room temperature in a tightly closed container; protect from moisture
pearls: Works by raising urinary citrate and urine pH (target pH 6.0-7.0, citrate >320 mg/day) to inhibit calcium and uric acid stone formation
Contraindicated in hyperkalemia or impaired potassium excretion (chronic renal failure) - potentially fatal hyperkalemia can be asymptomatic
Wax-matrix extended-release tablets are contraindicated with delayed GI transit and in peptic ulcer disease (GI lesion risk); ghost tablets in stool are expected
Avoid with potassium-sparing diuretics; monitor potassium with ACE inhibitors/ARBs/NSAIDs
Pair with low-salt diet and high fluid intake (urine output at least 2 L/day)
missed: Take the missed dose with food as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once. Consistent dosing maintains urinary alkalinization.
overdose: Overdose may cause hyperkalemia, which is often asymptomatic and may manifest only as increased serum potassium and characteristic ECG changes (peaked T waves, loss of P wave, ST depression, QT prolongation), with late muscle paralysis and cardiovascular collapse. Management includes cardiac/electrolyte monitoring; stopping potassium-containing and potassium-sparing agents; restricting dietary potassium; and standard hyperkalemia therapy (e.g., insulin/glucose, sodium bicarbonate, calcium for cardiac protection, and dialysis in renal failure).
